searchText: You generally shouldn't be holding secrets in your Ethereum client. Anything with a private key, really. It can be accounts (the keystore that is shipped with geth) or even the node key. that said, yes, you can certainly have your accounts managed elsewhere and only send signed transactions. You very much should not be giving private keys to the client. You may also want to have a cert for your http and ws connections. If it were up to me that "feature" would be removed from all clients. That's fine. Need a signer next to the client though then. Do you mean TLS certificate? If so, I think this should be managed by a reverse proxy. Do any of the clients actually support TLS natively? Besu does. But I think the point is more that there's a whole bunch of infrastructure around the client itself. In the same network perhaps, but I wouldn't put it "next to" the client I don't think (that is, not on same machine/container in most cases). The boundary of the deployment is not just the client, it's also how it can be accessed, etc. So the proxy would be part of the deployment. My preference is docker swarm with swarm secrets. I wouldn't switch over to kubernetes unless you go over like 100 servers (pretty large deployment). Prior to that, I don't think the complexity of kubernetes is worth it. I like traefik for reverse proxy and load balancing, because of its native integration with docker swarm and easy management. doesn't look like it will do repudiation, access control, and rotation. Gotta need Vault. ok let me look at traefik I use portainer as a UI into docker swarm and it *does* have access control. So you wouldn't need to give direct access to the swarm to everyone, just Portainer access and then use Portainer's ACL system for limiting who can access what keys. Note: I haven't used this particular feature of Portainer a lot, so definitely research the limits of its capabilities. In my experience, dealing with malicious actors *within* your infrastructure is really hard. I think in most situations it is more important to limit internal actors' ability to accidentally open security holes than it is to try to prevent them from being able to be malicious. yeah, looks like there is ACL with portainer: https://documentation.portainer.io/v2.0/secrets/add/ For example, making it hard to accidentally expose keys to the internet rather than trying to prevent an internal actor from going out of their way to steal keys. Of course, if the amount of money at risk is high enough, the calculus changes. <@!301186049323958275> it's not really up to me how this came about. Kube and Vault are the mandate. The big selling point of Vault is that you can request a token for usage that can be rescinded without ever divulging the secret. As for k8s, well, that's standard in my world. Our ops are better equipped for this. I have heard good things about Vault from an Enterprise standpoint. I never have used it personally though. same but it's hashicorp, and it's consul++ from what I get. Anyway. I'll keep your set up in mind for my own server over here 🙂 deploying in kubernetes shouldn't require referencing any external project like the helm chart above - there aren't that many things to configure - i can't see what value it would really create that you couldn't pretty easily whip up for your own use-case saying that with 5+ years kubernetes full time as a job vault integration would be wise - don't use kubernetes secrets directly for anything that is really sensitive oh I can do it in 5 minutes, sure. That's not really my point. In the video from Peter for example, you can see managing the health of a node is not trivial. I have picked up this little js for example that does something silly, and compare best known block to the best known block of infura: https://github.com/leapdao/eth-node-healthcheck/blob/master/index.js That's a sensible way to know if you're up to speed and can be used for querying. The besu nodes use a prometheus metric named in_sync that is set to 1 if there is less than 5 blocks to one of their peers best blocks. Check the latest block timestamp against now. If it is more than `n` minutes ago the node is probably unhealthy. that seems like a good enough approach that's also a good one, but time is not really a good indicator, if you have drift It lets you know when things are way off. It won't give you instant awareness of falling out of sync. or worse, you're on a branch, not on head... `n` needs to be like 5 minutes. A branch of mainnet is unlikely to be able to mine a block every 5 minutes. no that's not what I meant I meant - you get fresh blocks, but infura and the other nodes are on a different head. And at some point you're going to merge. If you have many nodes of different types, you can compare their heads against each other. E.g., nethermind+openethereum+Geth+besu. your node is being eclipsed! 🙂 even same type either way - you do need that 🙂 Then there is a good amount of customization you'd want to apply in terms of security hardening, like CORS, etc. So yes, ideally, because I'm lazy, I want a helm chart that does it all for me. Please don't judge me harshly 🙂 Are you trying to defend against a state actor level eclipse attack? Where there is enough hashpower to move the eclipse chain forward? I wasn't very serious just now? sorry. Internet forums. So that's the requirements I have right here. I am looking for a hardened setup for a redundant set of nodes that I can guarantee will run 24/7. with max security and kubernetes. spare no expense - load balancer in front of RPC serving nodes, advanced health check and health score, backups, secret management, metrics monitoring. What y'all got? I wasn't being clear, I realize now. You do need that, you do need this script that checks the timestamp of the head block and compares it to current time. And it needs to report somewhere that is then used to know whether to use that node for traffic. Like an advanced health check. What do you need to be doing with these nodes? Full nodes for data analysis ah, this is cool: https://ethereum.org/en/developers/tutorials/monitoring-geth-with-influxdb-and-grafana/
